passages.text: But if any of those present, though able to manage people’s unreasonableness, draws back, caring only for his own rest, let him too expect to hear, “Wicked and lazy servant, you should have put my silver before the bankers, and when I came I would have collected what was mine. Cast the useless servant into the outer darkness.” And rightly so. “For it was your responsibility,” he says, “human being, to put my words before bankers like silver and to test them like currency.” Therefore, the multitude of believers must obey one particular person, so that in this way it may be able to continue in harmony. For a system that culminates in the rule of a single authority, as an image of monarchy, puts those who submit in a position to enjoy peace because of good order; but when all are eager to rule and unwilling to yield to one alone, they are also certain to fall because of division.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διοικεῖν δυνάμενος τὴν ἀγνωμοσύνην τῶν ἀνθρώπων
lexical_decisions.chosen: though able to manage people’s unreasonableness
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here ἀγνωμοσύνη denotes deficient judgment or unreasonable conduct; “ingratitude” is lexically possible but fits the governing context less well.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Wicked and lazy servant
lexical_decisions.rationale: Following the supplied policy, δοῦλος is rendered “servant”; the context still carries the subordinate status of a servant answerable to his lord.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I would have collected what was mine
lexical_decisions.rationale: πράσσω here means exacting or recovering what is due, rather than merely “doing” what belongs to the speaker.

lexical_decisions.chosen: For it was your responsibility, he says, human being
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive σοῦ with the following infinitives is understood as an elliptical expression of obligation: “it was your part” or “it was your responsibility.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: to test them like currency
lexical_decisions.rationale: δοκιμάζω evokes testing or assaying currency; “them” refers to the preceding λόγους, though the Greek does not repeat the object.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ γὰρ εἰς ἀρχὴν μιᾶς λῆγον ἐξουσίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: a system that culminates in the rule of a single authority
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantivized neuter phrase describes an arrangement or system ending in one governing authority.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as an image of monarchy
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative εἰκόνι characterizes the single-authority arrangement as a likeness or representation of monarchy.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they are also certain to fall
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔχειν with an infinitive expresses what lies ahead or is inevitable; “they must also fall” is a viable alternative.

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a Greek question mark between χρήματα and δοκιμάσαι, interrupting two coordinated infinitives. The translation follows the defensible syntactic coordination while disclosing the punctuation rather than treating it as missing wording.

source_issues.source_quote: τὸ δὲ πάντας φιλαρχοῦντας ἑνὶ μόνῳ ὑπεῖξαι μὴ θέλειν, καὶ αἰτίᾳ διαιρέσεως πάντως καὶ πεσεῖν ἔχουσιν
source_issues.issue: The sentence begins with a neuter substantivized infinitival construction but shifts to the plural finite verb ἔχουσιν, with the semantic plural πάντας supplying the sense. This is intelligible as an anacoluthon, so no restoration is required.

passages.text: But furthermore, let what happens before our eyes persuade us: now, with many kings throughout the whole earth, wars happen continually. For each has the other’s rule as a pretext for war. But if one person is leader of the whole, having nothing for which to wage war, he has perpetual peace. Ultimately, then, for those deemed worthy of eternal life, God appoints one king over the whole in that age, so that, because of monarchy, unfailing peace may come about. Therefore, everyone must follow one person as guide, honoring him as an image of God, while the guide must know the entrance leading into the holy city.

lexical_decisions.chosen: let what happens before our eyes persuade us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb has no expressed object; “us” represents the assembled hearers, while “persuade the observer” or “be persuasive” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἔχει γὰρ ἕκαστος πρόφασιν εἰς πόλεμον τὴν ἑτέρου ἀρχήν
lexical_decisions.chosen: each has the other’s rule as a pretext for war
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόφασις may mean a pretext, occasion, or stated reason; “pretext” preserves the author’s critical force.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having nothing for which to wage war
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relative expression is understood impersonally as the absent reason or occasion for war; “having no one against whom to wage war” is a contextual alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Ultimately, then
lexical_decisions.rationale: πέρας functions adverbially as “at last,” “in the end,” or “as the final outcome,” introducing the eschatological arrangement.

lexical_decisions.chosen: unfailing peace
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἄπτωτος literally describes what does not fall or collapse; “secure peace” or “unshakable peace” are viable alternatives.

lexical_decisions.chosen: honoring him as an image of God
lexical_decisions.rationale: προτιμάω conveys assigning precedence or special honor; “preferring him” would be more literal but less clear in this context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς εἰς τὴν ἁγίαν πόλιν εἰσούσης εἰσόδου
lexical_decisions.chosen: the entrance leading into the holy city
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the source’s repeated entrance-and-entering image without reproducing an awkward English cognate construction.

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a period between the elided ἀλλ᾽ and ἔτι. It appears to be stray editorial punctuation rather than a lacuna marker; no wording has been supplied in its place.

passages.text: “Whom else among those present shall I choose except Zacchaeus, to whom our Lord also went in and rested, judging him worthy to be saved?” After saying this, he laid his hand on Zacchaeus, who was standing there, and pressed him to sit in his chair. But Zacchaeus fell at his feet and begged him to release him from governing, while making this promise and saying, “Whatever a leader must do, I will do; only grant me not to bear this name. For I am wary of putting on the name of office, for it is full of bitter envy and danger.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς ὃν καὶ ὁ κύριος ἡμῶν εἰσιὼν ἀνεπαύσατο
lexical_decisions.chosen: to whom our Lord also went in and rested
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording says that the Lord entered or went in to Zacchaeus and rested; it does not explicitly name a house.

lexical_decisions.chosen: judging him worthy to be saved
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive articular infinitive depends on ἄξιον and identifies that of which Zacchaeus was judged worthy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐβιάζετο ἐπὶ τὴν αὐτοῦ καθεσθῆναι καθέδραν
lexical_decisions.chosen: pressed him to sit in his chair
lexical_decisions.rationale: The middle verb can mean compel, constrain, or strongly urge. “Pressed” preserves the insistence without necessarily implying physical force.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to sit in his chair
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτοῦ most naturally refers to Zacchaeus, though Peter remains a grammatically possible referent; the English pronoun preserves that ambiguity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: release him from governing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive infinitive names the responsibility from which Zacchaeus asks to be released.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I am wary
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb may express caution, apprehension, or reverential fear; “I am afraid” is possible but somewhat stronger.

lexical_decisions.chosen: putting on the name of office
lexical_decisions.rationale: The translation retains the clothing image of ἐνδύομαι and renders ἀρχή as governing office in this context.

passages.text: And Peter said, “If this is what you are wary of, do not be called a ruler, but ‘the one appointed,’ since the Lord permitted this expression to be used when he said, ‘Blessed is that man whom his lord will appoint over the care of his fellow servants.’ If, however, you do not want it known at all that you have authority to administer, you seem to me not to realize that the acknowledged authority of the one presiding has considerable power to inspire deference in the multitude. For each person obeys one who has received the authority, since he regards his conscience as a powerful constraint. What then? Do you not also know for certain that you are to rule, not as the rulers of the nations do, but as a servant (ministering to them), as a father (to those being wronged), as a physician (attending to them), as a shepherd (guarding them)—in short, I say, having every concern for their salvation? Do you think I am unaware what sort of toils I am pressing you to undertake when I require you to be judged by crowds whom it is impossible for anyone to please? Yet one who acts well is fully able to win God’s favor. Therefore I ask you to undertake it willingly, for God’s sake, for the Messiah’s sake, for the salvation of the brothers, for their proper ordering, and for your benefit.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἄρχων μὲν μὴ καλοῦ, ἀλλὰ ὁ καθεστώς
lexical_decisions.chosen: do not be called a ruler, but ‘the one appointed’
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὁ καθεστώς is a perfect participial title meaning the person who has been established or appointed, deliberately distinguished from ἄρχων.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since the Lord permitted this expression to be used
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive absolute says that the Lord granted or allowed this designation to be spoken; “gave this to be said” would be more formally literal.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ τῆς θεραπείας τῶν συνδούλων αὐτοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: over the care of his fellow servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: θεραπεία can denote care, service, attendance, or a body of attendants. “Over the company of his fellow servants” is therefore possible, but “care” fits the ensuing description of pastoral duties.

lexical_decisions.chosen: fellow servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: Following the supplied policy, δοῦλος and its compound are rendered with “servant”; the compound stresses shared subordination to the same lord.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to inspire deference in the multitude
lexical_decisions.rationale: δυσωπία concerns restraint produced by respect, shame, or awe. “To overawe the multitude” is possible but gives the phrase a harsher tone.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς μεγάλην ἀνάγκην τὴν συνείδησιν ἔχων
lexical_decisions.chosen: since he regards his conscience as a powerful constraint
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle most naturally continues with ἕκαστος as its subject; conscience supplies the compelling reason to obey recognized authority.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐχ ὡς οἱ ἄρχοντες τῶν ἐθνῶν ἄρχειν ἔχεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: you are to rule, not as the rulers of the nations do
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔχεις with the infinitive expresses what Zacchaeus is expected or obliged to do.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Do you think I am unaware
lexical_decisions.rationale: The initial ὅτι introduces an elliptical rhetorical question; “Is it because you think I am unaware?” is a more explicit alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: when I require you to be judged by crowds
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀξιόω with an infinitive can mean require, expect, or deem appropriate, rather than necessarily “consider worthy.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: θεὸν δὲ εὖ πράττοντα πείθειν δυνατώτατον
lexical_decisions.chosen: Yet one who acts well is fully able to win God’s favor
lexical_decisions.rationale: The person acting well is taken as the subject of πείθειν and God as its object. More literally, “to persuade God” or “to prevail upon God” is possible; context favors the idiom of gaining divine approval.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for the Messiah’s sake
lexical_decisions.rationale: Χριστός functions independently as a title here, so it is rendered “the Messiah” under the supplied policy.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for their proper ordering
lexical_decisions.rationale: οἰκονομία can denote administration, management, arrangement, or stewardship. The genitive may be understood as the proper ordering or administration of the brothers.

passages.text: Also consider this other point: to the degree that administering the Messiah’s church involves toil and danger, the reward is that much greater. But furthermore, the punishment is also greater for one who is capable and disobeys. Therefore, knowing that you are more learned than those present, I want you to lend out the good counsels with which you have been entrusted by the Lord, so that you may hear, “Well done, good and faithful servant,” and not, like the one who hid the single talent, be found liable to punishment after receiving an accusation. But if you do not wish to become a good guardian of the church, identify someone else in your place, more learned and more faithful than you. But you will not provide one. For you were with the Lord, gave an account of the marvelous deeds, and learned how to administer a church.

lexical_decisions.chosen: administering the Messiah’s church
lexical_decisions.rationale: οἰκονομεῖν denotes managing or administering, and Χριστός is rendered as the independently functioning title “Messiah.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the reward is that much greater
lexical_decisions.rationale: τοσούτῳ supplies the proportional counterpart to the preceding toil and danger: the greater the burden, the greater the reward.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for one who is capable and disobeys
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantival participles describe someone able to accept the responsibility who nevertheless refuses or disobeys.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to lend out the good counsels
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering retains the financial metaphor of δανείζειν. γνώμαι may also be rendered “teachings,” “judgments,” or “principles.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: with which you have been entrusted by the Lord
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect passive treats the counsels as a trust committed to Zacchaeus by the Lord.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Well done, good and faithful servant
lexical_decisions.rationale: The isolated εὖ implies commendation, conventionally expressed in English as “Well done”; δοῦλος follows the supplied “servant” policy.

lexical_decisions.chosen: be found liable to punishment after receiving an accusation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔγκλημα is a charge, accusation, or ground of blame, and ἀναφανῇς means being shown or found to occupy the stated condition.

lexical_decisions.chosen: identify someone else in your place
lexical_decisions.rationale: μηνύω here means disclose, point out, or name a suitable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: But you will not provide one
lexical_decisions.rationale: The object is unexpressed but is supplied by the previously requested alternative person; “you will not produce one” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: gave an account of the marvelous deeds
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἱστορέω can mean inquire into, recount, or give a narrative account; the deeds are its expressed object here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: learned how to administer a church
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Greek uses the noun “administration” with “church”; the verbal English form expresses the acquired practical knowledge without adding a new claim.

source_issues.issue: The article and noun are feminine accusative plural, while θαυμασίους has the masculine accusative plural form under regular three-termination inflection. The intended sense remains clear, and the irregular agreement does not prevent a defensible translation.
